name: The Flood Register
description:
A live recording of the only full concert ever performed by Maren Solís-Ekwueme at the Crucible, a Circuit-tier venue in the old meatpacking district, captured on a single night in 2204. Solís-Ekwueme was known for refusing studio contracts and building her following entirely through live performance and pirate broadcasts; this recording, made by the venue's sound engineer on a consumer-grade rig, was released posthumously in 2207 after her death in a building collapse that many of her fans consider suspicious. The audio quality is imperfect — crowd noise leaks into every track, there are two moments where feedback shrieked through the monitors, and the room's acoustics were never designed for this kind of music. None of this diminishes it.

Standout tracks include 'Estuary Road,' a twenty-two-minute improvised piece in which Solís-Ekwueme moves from sparse fingerpicked guitar into a full-band eruption, her voice shifting between three languages mid-phrase in a way that feels less like code-switching and more like thought; 'Cartography of Debts,' a quiet, devastating song about her grandmother's displacement from the coastal zones, which caused audible weeping in the crowd that the recording captures; and the final track, 'Register,' performed alone after the band left the stage, just her voice and a single sustained synthesizer tone, the last two minutes of which were recorded in near-total silence as the audience refused to make a sound.
creator: Maren Solís-Ekwueme
audience: Circuit workers, the Gray Zone residents who knew her work, folk and roots music communities across all tiers, anyone who experienced the 2190s coastal displacement migrations
cultural_impact: The Flood Register has become one of the most-copied recordings in GLMZ's underground music ecosystem, passed on data chips, pirate neural-feeds, and worn-out physical pressings. Solís-Ekwueme's death — officially attributed to structural failure in a Tier 2 residential block — has never been fully investigated, and a persistent faction of her followers believes a Vantablack Media subsidiary was involved after she publicly refused three separate recording contracts. The album's gray-market status means it exists in a legal limbo: not officially banned but not licensed, the estate's rights claimed by competing parties. It has been cited as an influence by more than forty subsequent artists across the Gray Zone and Circuit.
known_fans: coastal displacement community survivors and descendants
story_hooks: The original recording rig — a consumer-grade unit that captured the concert — has surfaced in a pawn shop in the Circuit, and it contains thirty minutes of pre-show audio that was never released, including what sounds like a heated argument between Solís-Ekwueme and an unidentified man in a corporate access badge.

A Vantablack Media subsidiary has filed a legal claim on the posthumous album's distribution rights, and the sound engineer who made the recording is being pressured to hand over the original files — he has gone to ground and is asking for help.

A young musician who is Solís-Ekwueme's daughter has never heard her mother perform and does not know the album exists; finding her and delivering a copy is a simple job that becomes complicated when someone else is also looking for her.
